facts.quote: The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions lend balances at the Federal Reserve to other depository institutions overnight.
facts.claim: The fed funds rate is the overnight rate banks charge each other to lend the balances they keep at the Fed.

facts.quote: The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings per year.
facts.claim: The FOMC has eight scheduled meetings a year.

facts.quote: The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings during the year and other meetings as needed.
facts.claim: Eight scheduled FOMC meetings a year, plus extra meetings when needed (calendar page, last updated October 28, 2026).

facts.quote: so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.
facts.claim: The Federal Reserve Act gives the Fed the goals of maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates.

facts.quote: Even though the act lists three distinct goals of monetary policy, the Fed's mandate for monetary policy is commonly known as the dual mandate.
facts.claim: The Fed's goals are known as the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices.

facts.quote: low and stable inflation at the rate of 2 percent per year, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with achievement of both parts of the dual mandate.
facts.claim: The FOMC's inflation goal is 2% a year, measured by the PCE price index.

facts.quote: Aiming for inflation that is a little above zero will, in normal times, result in modestly higher interest rates than would aiming for zero inflation.
facts.claim: Aiming a little above zero inflation keeps normal-time interest rates a bit higher than a zero goal would.

facts.quote: The higher level of interest rates in normal times gives the FOMC more room to cut interest rates to support the economy when it weakens.
facts.claim: Those higher normal-time rates leave the FOMC room to cut when the economy weakens.

facts.quote: The federal funds rate is the interest rate that banks pay to borrow reserve balances overnight.
facts.claim: Fed funds is the rate banks pay to borrow reserves overnight.

facts.quote: The FOMC's primary means of adjusting the stance of monetary policy is by changing its target for the federal funds rate.
facts.claim: The FOMC's main tool is its target for the fed funds rate.

facts.claim: Short-term rates such as Treasury bill yields typically move closely with the fed funds rate.

walkthroughs.title: Who sets the rate
steps: Banks lend each other reserves overnight. The rate they pay is the fed funds rate, the one Fed headlines are about.
The Fed's FOMC sets a target range for it. They meet eight times a year on the calendar.
What they're after is the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices, with inflation at 2% a year.
T-bill yields move right with that rate. Longer yields also price where it's expected to go.

walkthroughs.title: Reading the curve
steps: Line up Treasury yields from the shortest maturity to the longest. That's the yield curve.
Normally it slopes up. January 3, 2022, the 2-year paid 0.78% and the 10-year paid 1.63%.
The 2s10s is the 10-year yield minus the 2-year. Below zero, the curve is inverted there.
Fast forward to December 30, 2022. The 2-year paid 4.41%, the 10-year 3.88%. Inverted.

walkthroughs.title: 2022, the year of hikes
steps: 2022. The Fed's range starts the year at 0% to 0.25% and ends at 4.25% to 4.5%. Seven hikes.
The market didn't wait for them. Yields rose and stocks fell before the first hike in March.
By year-end the tech-heavy Nasdaq was down 33.1%.
Why tech got hit harder: growth stocks lean on profits years out. A higher rate shrinks what those are worth today.

questions.q: It's Fed day, 2:00 p.m., and a new target range for fed funds just came out. Who set it?
questions.why: The FOMC, the Fed's rate-setting committee. It sets the target range, and moving that target is its main tool. Then banks trade fed funds with each other overnight. The volume-weighted median of those trades is the effective rate. So the committee sets the range, and the banks trade inside it. Congress gave the Fed its goals. It doesn't pick the number, and neither does Treasury. Every rate headline you read on Fed day traces back to that one committee.
questions.lesson_line: The FOMC sets the range. The banks trade inside it.

wrong.The Treasury: Treasury borrows by selling bonds and bills. It doesn't set the Fed's rate.
wrong.Congress: Congress wrote the Fed's goals into the Federal Reserve Act. The number itself is the FOMC's call.
wrong.Bank trading: Close, but that's the effective rate, set by trading each day. The range it trades in is the FOMC's call.

questions.simple: The FOMC, the Fed's rate-setting committee, sets the target range. Banks then trade inside it.

questions.q: A headline says the Fed raised the federal funds rate. Which rate did it actually move?
questions.why: The overnight rate banks pay to borrow from each other. Banks keep reserve balances at the Fed, and they lend those balances to each other overnight. That's the rate the Fed targets, and moving that target is its main tool. T-bill yields move right along with it. It's not your mortgage rate or the 10-year yield. Those are long-term rates, and they price where policy is headed, not just where it sits tonight. So when you hear the Fed hiked, it's the overnight rate that moved. The long end does its own thing.
questions.lesson_line: Fed funds is the overnight bank rate. That's the one the Fed sets.

wrong.The 10-year Treasury yield: That's a long-term market yield. The Fed targets the overnight rate, and the 10-year moves on expectations.
wrong.The 30-year mortgage rate: Mortgages are long loans. Their rates price where policy is expected to go, not just tonight's rate.
wrong.The Fed's yearly inflation goal: That's the target for inflation, what policy aims at. Fed funds is a rate banks pay to borrow.

questions.simple: It's the rate banks charge each other to borrow overnight. That's the rate the Fed aims at.

questions.q: Fill in the blank.
questions.sentence: The Fed's dual mandate is maximum employment and stable ___.
questions.why: Prices. The Federal Reserve Act lists maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates. Even so, the mandate is commonly known as the dual mandate. Stable prices means low, steady inflation, not steady stock prices.
questions.lesson_line: Jobs and prices. When inflation runs hot, the Fed leans on rates.
questions.simple: Prices. The Fed's two goals are lots of jobs and steady prices, meaning low, steady inflation.

questions.q: The Fed has a scheduled rate meeting every month, twelve a year.
questions.why: False, it's eight. The FOMC has eight scheduled meetings a year, plus extra ones if it needs them. So plenty of months have no Fed day at all. The dates are posted well ahead on the Fed's calendar page, so put them on yours. I don't have a Fed-day rule, honestly. I trade those days like any other day. I just want to know one's coming, so a fast afternoon doesn't surprise me.
questions.lesson_line: Eight scheduled meetings a year, plus extras if needed. The dates are on the Fed's calendar.
questions.simple: False. The Fed has eight planned meetings a year, not twelve, and it can add extra ones.

reasons: the meeting schedule is a practice that can change (checked live 2026-11-12)

questions.q: Zero inflation is the Fed's goal.
questions.why: False. The goal is 2% a year, measured by the PCE price index. It isn't zero for a reason. Aiming a little above zero keeps rates a bit higher in normal times. That leaves the Fed room to cut when the economy weakens. If rates already sat near zero, there'd be nothing left to cut. Here's why you care. When the Fed says inflation is well above 2%, hikes are likely on the way. It said exactly that in January 2022, and the first hike landed in March.
questions.lesson_line: The Fed wants 2%, not zero. That cushion leaves it room to cut.
questions.simple: False. The Fed aims for 2% inflation, which keeps rates high enough to leave room to cut.

reasons: the inflation goal is a policy that can change (checked live 2026-11-12)

questions.q: Someone in the chat says "the 2s10s just went negative." What are they measuring?
questions.why: The 10-year yield minus the 2-year yield. Long minus short. FRED builds its 10-year minus 2-year series exactly that way, and Fed researchers call it the 2s10s. It tells you the slope between those two points, not how high rates are. Above zero is the normal upward slope. Below zero, the 2-year pays more than the 10-year, so the curve is inverted there. To check it yourself, pull up FRED's T10Y2Y chart.
questions.lesson_line: Long minus short. Above zero is normal, below zero is inverted.

wrong.2-year yield minus 10-year yield: That flips the sign. It's long minus short, so an inversion reads negative.
wrong.Fed funds minus the 10-year yield: Some researchers pair the 10-year with fed funds, but that's a different spread. The 2s10s uses two Treasury yields.
wrong.Average of the 2- and 10-year yields: An average tells you the level of rates. The 2s10s is the gap between them, the slope.

questions.simple: It's the 10-year yield minus the 2-year yield, the gap between long and short rates.

questions.q: When the curve is inverted, short-term Treasurys pay more than long-term ones.
questions.why: True. Normally the curve slopes up, so you get paid more to lend for longer. Inverted flips that, and the short maturities yield more than the long ones. One catch though. Different spreads can invert at different times. A curve can be inverted between two points and still normal between two others. So when someone tells you the curve inverted, ask them which part.
questions.lesson_line: Inverted means short pays more than long. Always ask which part.
questions.simple: True. Inverted means short-term bonds pay more than long-term ones, the reverse of normal.

questions.q: You're holding a few swings into a Fed decision day. When does the statement hit?
questions.sentence: On Fed day, the FOMC statement comes out at ___ Eastern.
questions.why: 2:00 p.m. Eastern, EST or EDT depending on the season. That's when the statement drops on a decision day. Not the open, not the close, right in the middle of the afternoon. Prices can move fast in the minutes after. Your stops are already in, so there's nothing special to do. Just know the clock, so a 2:00 spike doesn't catch you guessing what happened.
questions.lesson_line: Fed statements hit at 2:00 p.m. Eastern. Know the time, then trade your setups.
questions.simple: The Fed's statement comes out at 2:00 p.m. Eastern on decision day.

reasons: release time is a practice that can change (checked live on the October 28, 2026 statement)

questions.q: The Fed just hiked 75 basis points. How many percentage points did the rate go up?
questions.why: 0.75 points. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point. So 75 divided by 100 is 0.75. On TV you'll hear it called three-quarters of a point, same thing. It's a move in the rate itself, not a 75% jump in the rate. The Fed made this exact move in 2022. One 75 basis point hike took the range from 1.50-1.75% to 2.25-2.50%.
questions.lesson_line: 100 basis points make one point. A 25 basis point move is a quarter point.
questions.simple: It's 0.75 points. 100 basis points make one point.

deeper.example: The Fed's own table shows one: a 75 basis point hike took the target range from 1.50-1.75% to 2.25-2.50%. Each end rose 0.75 percentage points.

wrong.7.5 points: Moved the decimal one place too few. 75 over 100 is 0.75.
wrong.0.075 points: Moved the decimal one place too many. 75 over 100 is 0.75.
wrong.75 points: Left the basis points as they were. Divide by 100 to get points.

questions.q: January 3, 2022. The 2-year Treasury yields 0.78% and the 10-year 1.63%. Where's the 2s10s?
questions.why: 0.85 points, and positive. Long minus short: 1.63 minus 0.78 is 0.85. Positive means the curve sloped up between those two points, the normal shape. Remember where you are on the calendar. The Fed's rate still sat near zero, and the hikes hadn't started. Keep this number in mind, because by the end of that year the spread was below zero.
questions.lesson_line: Always long minus short. Above zero is the normal, upward slope.
questions.simple: It's 0.85, the 10-year's 1.63 minus the 2-year's 0.78, so the curve sloped up.

wrong.-0.85 points: Flipped it. That's the 2-year minus the 10-year. Always long minus short.
wrong.2.41 points: Added the two yields. The spread is a gap, so you subtract.
wrong.1.63 points: That's just the 10-year yield. You still have to take off the 2-year.

questions.q: When the Fed hikes hard, the 10-year yield climbs about as much as the Fed's rate.
questions.why: False. The Fed moves the short end. The 10-year prices where policy and the economy are expected to go, so in a tightening it rises less. 2022 shows it clearly. The top of the Fed's range went from 0.25% to 4.5%, a 4.25 point climb. The 10-year went from 1.63% to 3.88%, about half the Fed's move. That gap between the short end and the long end is exactly what flattens the curve when the Fed hikes.
questions.lesson_line: The Fed moves the short end. The long end moves on expectations.
questions.simple: False. The 10-year moves on where rates are expected to go, so it climbs less than the Fed's rate.

questions.story: The curve starts with a normal upward slope. The Fed hikes at meeting after meeting. The 2-year yield climbs fast. The 10-year rises far less.
questions.q: Where's the 2s10s heading?
choices: Inverts as soon as hikes start
questions.why: It shrinks, and the curve flattens. The 2s10s is the 10-year minus the 2-year. When the 2-year runs and the 10-year lags, that gap gets smaller. That's what Fed hiking does. Short yields chase the Fed, and long yields move on expectations. It only inverts if the 2-year actually climbs past the 10-year, so flattening comes first. You can watch it happen on FRED's 10-year minus 2-year chart as the line slides toward zero.
questions.lesson_line: Hiking cycles flatten the curve. Keep hiking and it can invert.

wrong.Widens, the curve steepens: Steepening means the 10-year gains on the 2-year. Here the 2-year is the one running.
wrong.Stays put, both yields rose: The 2s10s is a gap, not a level. When the 2-year rises more, the gap shrinks.
wrong.Inverts as soon as hikes start: Not right away. It flattens first, and it only inverts once the 2-year climbs above the 10-year.

questions.simple: The gap shrinks, because the 2-year yield rises much faster than the 10-year yield.

deeper.trap: The answer depends on where the curve starts. From a normal, upward slope, a shrinking 2s10s means flattening. If the curve were already inverted, the same moves would push it further below zero.

questions.q: The Fed's range starts 2022 at 0-0.25% and ends the year at 4.25-4.50%. How much did the top end climb?
questions.why: 4.25 points. The top end went from 0.25% to 4.50%, and 4.50 minus 0.25 is 4.25. It took seven hikes: 25, 50, 75, 75, 75, 75 and 50 basis points. Add those up and you land on the same 4.25 points. It left the Fed's rate at its highest in 15 years. Keep that in your head as the backdrop for what happened to growth stocks that year.
questions.lesson_line: In 2022 the Fed went from near zero to 4.25-4.5% in seven hikes, its highest in 15 years.
questions.simple: The top end rose 4.25 points, from 0.25% to 4.50%.

deeper.example: The Fed's table lists the seven hikes: 25, 50, 75, 75, 75, 75 and 50 basis points. They add up to the same 4.25 points.

wrong.4.50 points: That's just December's top end. Subtract where it started, 0.25.
wrong.4.75 points: You added the 0.25 instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: Rates jump in 2022, and fast growers that still lose money get crushed. Why were they hit so hard?
choices: Most of their profit is years away
Their sales drop as rates rise
questions.answer: Most of their profit is years away
questions.why: Most of their profit is years away. Here's how it works. A higher rate shrinks what future cash flows are worth today. If most of a company's value sits in earnings years out, that discount hits it harder. In 2022 the market said it plainly: stop paying up for unprofitable growth, show me cash. The tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 33.1% that year. The lesson for you is where to look. When rates rip, don't cling to last cycle's winners. Find what's still holding up.
questions.lesson_line: Far-off profits get discounted harder when rates rise. That's why 2022 crushed unprofitable growth.

wrong.They pay the biggest dividends: Companies still losing money have little to pay out. The hit came through valuations.
wrong.Their sales drop as rates rise: Rate changes usually take at least 12 months to reach the wider economy. Stocks react way sooner, through valuations.
wrong.The Fed targeted tech stocks: The Fed doesn't pick sectors. It hikes to cool the economy, and growth stocks feel it through valuations.

questions.simple: Their profits are far off, and higher rates make far-off profits worth less today.

deeper.counter: Higher rates don't automatically mean lower stock prices. Schwab says why rates rise, how fast, and earnings matter more. And 2022 also had sticky inflation and Russia's invasion of Ukraine weighing on stocks.

reasons: fixed before (q14 stem and why, 2026-11-09); sources differ on growth-stock sensitivity (see conflicts)

questions.q: Before the Fed's first hike of 2022, Treasury yields were already rising and stocks were already falling.
questions.why: True, and this SPY chart shows the stock side of it. The first hike didn't come until March. But the market started pricing it in during the third quarter of the year before. Treasury yields, corporate bond yields and mortgage rates all started climbing. Broad stock indexes fell. So by the time the Fed moved, a lot of the damage was done. Price leads the news. I'd rather read what the market is doing than wait for the Fed to announce it.
questions.lesson_line: Price leads the news. By the time the Fed moves, a lot is already priced.
questions.simple: True. Markets moved early, so yields rose and stocks fell before the first hike.

questions.story: Fed funds futures are pricing a 50 basis point cut. At 2:00 the Fed cuts 25 instead. Stocks sell off.
questions.q: Why would a rate cut sink stocks?
choices: The bigger cut was already priced in
Any cut means the economy is failing
Lower rates make stocks less attractive
Stocks fall whenever the Fed acts
questions.answer: The bigger cut was already priced in
questions.why: The bigger cut was already priced in. The market mostly trades the surprise, not the cut. Futures said 50, so prices already had 50 baked in. The Fed gave 25. That's less easing than everyone bet on, so stocks likely reprice lower. It works the other way too: a surprise cut has tended to lift stocks. Before any Fed day, check CME's FedWatch. It turns fed funds futures into odds for each move, so you know what's priced.
questions.lesson_line: Markets trade the surprise, not the headline. What's priced sets the bar.

wrong.Any cut means the economy is failing: A cut can come with a weak economy, but that's not the story here. The miss versus 50 is the news.
wrong.Lower rates make stocks less attractive: Backwards. Lower rates can make stocks more attractive. The problem was the size.
wrong.Stocks fall whenever the Fed acts: A move the market already expected barely registers, and a surprise cut has tended to lift stocks.

questions.simple: Traders had already bet on a bigger cut, so the smaller one let them down and stocks fell.

deeper.example: Flip it. Fed research looked at surprise 25 basis point cuts. On average, such a cut went with about a one percent rise in broad stock indexes. Same kind of cut, opposite reaction: what matters is the gap between what was priced and what came.

questions.q: What's the curve telling you here?
questions.why: The 2s10s is inverted, the 10y-3m isn't. Work it through. The 10-year at 2.93% sits just under the 2-year at 2.97%, so the 2s10s is below zero. But the 10-year is way above the 3-month at 1.90%, so that spread is still positive. Same curve, same day, two different answers. The 2s10s tends to flip first, and more often. So when you see a headline that the curve inverted, ask which spread they mean.
questions.lesson_line: When you hear the curve inverted, ask which spread. The 2s10s flips first.

wrong.Both spreads are inverted: The 10-year at 2.93% still pays more than the 3-month at 1.90%. That one's positive.
wrong.Normal, long yields beat short: Not against the 2-year. The 10-year at 2.93% is under the 2-year at 2.97%.
wrong.10y-3m inverted, 2s10s positive: You mixed them up. The 10-year beats the 3-month but trails the 2-year.

questions.simple: The 10-year pays a bit less than the 2-year, so the 2s10s is inverted, but it still beats the 3-month.

deeper.trap: A headline that says the curve inverted may mean only the 2s10s. On this day the 10-year still paid more than the 3-month. The 2s10s tends to turn negative earlier and more often than the 10-year minus 3-month, so always ask which spread.

reasons: key rests on one Treasury row (f40)

questions.q: You pull up the New York Fed's recession-odds model. Which spread is it built on?
questions.why: The 10-year minus the 3-month. The New York Fed takes the 10-year bond rate minus the 3-month bill rate. It turns that spread into the odds of a recession twelve months out. That's not the spread you hear about most. Market folks mostly watch the 10-year minus the 2-year, and some researchers use the 10-year against fed funds. Why you care: the 2s10s flips earlier and more often than the 10y-3m. Two people can look at the curve and see different things, so know which one you're reading.
questions.lesson_line: Headlines watch the 2s10s. The New York Fed's model uses the 10-year minus the 3-month.

wrong.10-year minus 2-year: That's the market's favorite, not the model's input. It tends to invert earlier and more often.
wrong.30-year minus 10-year: That's the far end of the curve. The model pairs the 10-year with a short bill rate.
wrong.10-year minus fed funds: Some researchers like that pair. The New York Fed's model uses the 3-month bill rate instead.

questions.simple: It uses the 10-year rate minus the 3-month bill rate to estimate the odds of a recession.

deeper.trap: The model gives odds, not a verdict. It turns the spread into a recession probability for twelve months ahead, using monthly averages.

reasons: key rests on one Tier 1 fact (f37)
the model's input could change (checked live: PDF updated 05-Nov-2026)

questions.q: 2022: the Fed hikes seven times. Which of these took the worst beating on the year?
questions.why: The Nasdaq Composite. The tech-heavy index lost 33.1%, its steepest drop since 2008. The S&P 500 lost 19.4%, or 18.1% with dividends. The Dow held up best of the three, down 8.8%. Energy stocks went the other way, up 59% as oil jumped above $120. That's what a rate-hike bear market looks like. The high-priced tech names got sold the hardest. If you were hunting for strength that year, you weren't finding it in tech.
questions.lesson_line: In 2022's rate-hike bear market, tech and growth took the worst of it.

wrong.The Dow industrials: The Dow held up best of the three indexes, down 8.8%.
wrong.S&P 500 energy stocks: Energy went the other way, up 59% in 2022 as oil jumped above $120.
wrong.The S&P 500 index: It fell 19.4%, or 18.1% with dividends. Bad, but the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 33.1%.

questions.simple: The tech-heavy Nasdaq fell the most, down 33.1%, as rising rates hit tech and growth stocks.

deeper.trap: Check which measure a figure uses. AP gives the S&P 500's 2022 price change as 19.4%, but 18.1% with dividends. Compare price change with price change, never with a total return.

questions.story: The 2s10s closes below zero for one session, then pops right back. Someone in the chat says the recession is locked in.
questions.q: How much weight do you give that dip?
questions.why: Not much. One day under zero is the kind of reading New York Fed research says often turns out false. Inversions that hold on monthly or quarterly averages are the ones worth respecting. Even a lasting inversion is a warning, not a start date. It mostly reflects what the market already expects. So I'm not changing how I trade over one print. Price, the leaders and the market reading in our app tell me far more.
questions.lesson_line: One day under zero proves nothing. Respect inversions that hold on monthly averages.

wrong.Full weight, any dip counts: Daily inversions often prove false. The ones that hold on monthly or quarterly averages count more.
wrong.A recession began today: An inversion is a warning, not a start date. The New York Fed's model gives recession odds twelve months ahead.
wrong.Heavy, it means recession: Not off one session. Fed Board researchers say an inversion is no standalone recession call.

questions.simple: Give it little weight. A one-day dip below zero often turns out to be a false alarm.

deeper.trap: One session below zero is the kind of daily reading the research calls often false. Look for an inversion that holds on monthly or quarterly averages. Even then it is a warning, not a date.

questions.story: Over 2022 the 2-year Treasury yield rose from 0.78% to 4.41%. The 10-year rose from 1.63% to 3.88%.
questions.q: Where did the 2s10s finish the year?
questions.why: -0.53, inverted. Long minus short: 3.88 minus 4.41 is -0.53. The 2-year went from 0.78% to 4.41% as it chased the Fed. The 10-year only went from 1.63% to 3.88%. The short end ran right past the long end, and the curve flipped upside down. You started the year at +0.85, so the spread fell 1.38 points in twelve months. That's the flattening you learned about, carried all the way through zero.
questions.lesson_line: Short yields chased the Fed in 2022. That's what turned the curve upside down.

wrong.+0.53, normal slope: That's 2-year minus 10-year. The 2s10s is long minus short, so it's negative.
wrong.+0.85, unchanged: That's where it started the year, 1.63 minus 0.78. The year-end yields give a different answer.
wrong.-1.38, far inverted: That's how far the spread fell over the year, from +0.85. The year-end level is what you want.

questions.simple: It ended at -0.53, because the 2-year yield rose past the 10-year yield.

questions.story: The Fed hikes 25 basis points, exactly what futures priced. But the statement signals more hikes ahead than the market expected.
questions.q: What's the real news for stocks?
choices: The higher expected path of rates
The hike makes stocks more attractive
questions.answer: The higher expected path of rates
questions.why: The higher expected path of rates. The 25 basis point hike was old news. Futures had it priced, and markets barely react to a move they already expected. The surprise was in the statement. More hikes ahead than people thought means a higher path of rates, and that moves prices on its own. Higher expected rates shrink what future cash flows are worth today. So don't stop at a headline like "Fed hikes as expected." Read what they said about what comes next.
questions.lesson_line: A priced-in hike is old news. The surprise is the path.

wrong.The 25 basis point hike itself: It was fully priced. Markets barely react to a move they already expected.
wrong.Nothing, the hike was expected: The hike was, the path wasn't. A shift in the expected path moves prices on its own.
wrong.The hike makes stocks more attractive: Backwards. Lower rates can make stocks more attractive. A higher path of rates is the headwind here.

questions.simple: The hike was already expected, so the news was the Fed hinting at more hikes than traders thought.

deeper.trap: A headline like Fed hikes as expected can hide the real move. The statement's words about future rates can be the surprise. Higher expected rates shrink what future cash flows are worth today.

questions.q: After the 2s10s inverted in July 2022, a US recession followed within a year.
questions.why: False, and it's a good one to remember. The 2s10s inverted in early July 2022 and stayed inverted for a record run. It outlasted the old record, a 624-day inversion in 1978. And no recession came. NBER's latest call is still the April 2020 trough, so none has been dated since. An inversion is a warning, not a timer. Don't build a trade, or a pile of cash, around a countdown the curve never promised.
questions.lesson_line: An inversion is a warning, not a timer.
questions.simple: False. The curve stayed inverted from July 2022 for a record run, and no recession came.

deeper.counter: This does not make inversions useless. Fed Board researchers say an inverted spread is not a standalone recession call: it largely reflects what markets already expect. Read the curve with other evidence, never as a countdown.

reasons: rests on NBER's dating, which can change (checked live 2026-11-12: latest call still July 19, 2021)

questions.q: From June 2022 into early 2023, broad stock indexes rose on net while the Fed was still hiking.
questions.why: True, and you can see it on this SPY chart. The Fed's own report says broad indexes rose moderately, on net, from June 2022, with plenty of chop along the way. Inflation showed signs of easing and earnings held up. Meanwhile the Fed kept hiking, all the way to 4.25-4.5% in December. Rising rates don't automatically mean falling stocks. The market looks ahead, and it can turn before the Fed stops. That's why I don't wait for the Fed's all-clear. I watch price.
questions.lesson_line: The market looks ahead. It can turn up before the Fed stops hiking.
questions.simple: True. Stocks rose on net from June 2022, even while the Fed kept raising rates.

deeper.trap: On net matters. The Fed's report says indexes were volatile while they rose. A market can trend up through a hiking cycle and still swing hard along the way.

conflicts: Growth stocks and rising rates: Schwab (s25, October 2026) says 'Cyclical sectors and high-growth stocks have tended to be less sensitive to rising interest rates', while also explaining that long-duration growth stocks may face valuation pressure at higher discount rates (f64). Investopedia (s30) says the impact on valuations 'is often more pronounced for growth stocks that derive more of their value from expected future earnings' (f89), yet also that when the Fed raises rates 'toward the end of a boom cycle' technology and growth stocks 'often continue to do well'. In 2022 the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell hardest (AP, CNBC). The file teaches the discount-rate mechanism with 'often' and 'may', frames q14 on 2022 (barely profitable growth), never 'always', and q24 teaches that rising rates do not automatically mean falling stocks (f65, f29). Checker 2026-11-09: q14's why no longer says long-dated profits 'take the biggest hit' (no source says 'biggest'); it now rests on f64 + f89.

Which spread to watch: the Fed Board's FEDS Note (s22) argues the 2-10 spread 'offers a particularly muddled view' and that inversions are not independent recession measures; Investopedia (s31) calls the 10-year/2-year spread a relatively reliable recession indicator. The file never keys the 2s10s as reliable: it asks which spread the NY Fed model uses (Tier 1, s14), teaches that brief inversions mislead (s21 + s31), and uses the 2022-24 record (q23).

Investopedia's inverted-yield-curve page (s31) states the December 30, 2022 spread 'was 53 percentage points' and a 2026 spread '36 percentage points'; these should read basis points (Treasury's own rows give 3.88% minus 4.41% = -0.53 points). The file takes every yield from Treasury's rows (s15-s17) and cites no Investopedia number.

Effective fed funds rate: FRED's FEDFUNDS notes (s11) call it a 'weighted average'; the New York Fed, which publishes it, says 'volume-weighted median' (s13). The file uses only the New York Fed wording, and only in a wrong-choice note (q01).

The Fed's Open Market Operations table (s4) dates each change the day after the decision (March 17, 2022 versus the March 16 statement; its note corrects March 3, 2020 to March 4). The file takes dates from the statements and uses the table only for the count and size of the 2022 hikes.

Spread measures: Treasury's 3-month par-curve yield (q17) is a constant-maturity rate; the NY Fed model uses the secondary-market 3-month bill on a bond-equivalent basis (s21). The file reads Treasury's own numbers and never claims the NY Fed's monthly reading for a day.

Current policy, as of 2026-11-09: the Fed raised its range 25 basis points in September 2026 (to 3.75-4.00%, s4) and held it at 3-3/4 to 4 percent on October 28, 2026 (s8). Not quizzed: it changes every six weeks or so.

Track audit 2026-11-09: 2022 figures differ by measure across the track. AP (s27) gives price changes: S&P 500 -19.4% ('or 18.1%, including dividends', f69), energy stocks +59% and 'the only gain among the 11 sectors'. F7.09 uses the Select Sector prospectus's total returns: S&P 500 -18.11%, energy +64.56%, utilities +1.57%. With dividends utilities also rose, so q19's wrong note and f72's claim no longer say energy was the only sector up, and q19's S&P 500 note gives both AP figures. q24 and f29 now keep the Fed's 'on net': the S&P 500 made a lower close in October 2022 than in June (F7.04, F7.08).
